text.p: Poland's ruling coalition began a major reorganisation of ministries on Tuesday but the dominant social democrats had to sacrifice their reformist privatisation minister to win their Peasant Party partner's cooperation.

The ex-minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek, widely seen as a champion of pro-market policies, was persuaded by his party chiefs to take the post of deputy minister in charge of privatisation in a new treasury ministry.

In the first of a series of changes aimed at streamlining administration, the powerful treasury ministry came into being at midnight, taking in the privatisation portfolio held by Kaczmarek of the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD).

In a compromise with the smaller Polish Peasant Party (PSL) -- which has often criticised sales of state assets -- the more reformist SLD conceded the new ministry to the Peasants' Miroslaw Pietrewicz, who had been head of the planning ministry.
Anxious to ensure privatisation remained on track despite the concession, SLD chiefs asked the reluctant Kaczmarek to accept the junior post and he was appointed alongside Pietrewicz on Tuesday.

"I am very pleased that...the treasury ministry leadership will embrace Wieslaw Kaczmarek, who over the last three years conducted a heroic struggle to ensure the privatisation process brought the desired results," President Aleksander Kwasniewski, linked to the SLD, said at the swearing-in ceremony.
The replacement of Kaczmarek, who has steered Poland's gradual sales of state assets since the two parties won 1993 elections, had raised SLD fears privatisation could slow down.
Privatisation is a key to crucial further reforms, especially as a source of capital for new pension funds to replace the inefficient and costly social security system.
Kaczmarek earlier expressed strong reluctance to take the deputy post, saying he had spoken with Pietrewicz who had failed to spell out his exact intentions.
"This compromise...led to the better being replaced by the worse," Kaczmarek told the leftist daily Trybuna.
Kaczmarek has broadly implemented policies worked out by Solidarity-rooted governments after the 1989 fall of communism, although the centrist opposition says he has gone too slowly.

Apart from individual sales of key enterprises, he steered last year's launch of a Mass Privatisation Programme under which 500 firms have been grouped under 15 National Investment Funds, stakes in which have been sold to the public.
In his new capacity Kaczmarek will continue to oversee such matters as well as restructuring state enterprises.

His party has staunchly defended him against attacks from a faction of the Peasant Party, also rooted in the old communist system, which accused him of selling national assets too cheaply. His latest appointment showed the SLD continued to stand by him.

The two parties, often jostling for posts in government, have struck a deal to fill the new ministries being created under the administrative reform, so as to preserve the creaking coalition until parliamentary elections in late 1997.

Under the coalition deal, the SLD will get the economy ministry, which will replace the industry and foreign trade porfolios on January 1, and will also keep the crucial interior ministry which will be expanded at the same time.

The prime minister's authority will grow -- for example he will take responsiblity for the security service. Some tasks, including oversight of about 1,200 remaining state firms, will devolve to the provinces which already control 1,500.
